content: Consumers, including heavy drinkers and young individuals, are highly responsive to changes in the price of alcoholic beverages. Pricing policies can be strategically employed to reduce underage drinking, prevent the escalation of alcohol consumption to harmful levels, and influence consumer preferences. Increasing the price of alcoholic beverages is one of the most effective interventions to mitigate the harmful use of alcohol. The success of price-related policies in reducing alcohol-related harm is heavily dependent on the implementation of an efficient taxation system, coupled with robust tax collection and enforcement mechanisms. The harmful use of alcohol is a significant risk factor for the global burden of disease and injuries. Alcohol consumption is causally linked to over 200 health conditions, including mental and behavioral disorders, major noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), road traffic accidents, violence, and suicides. Additionally, alcohol misuse adversely affects the development and treatment outcomes of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS. The impact of harmful alcohol use extends beyond the drinker, often causing devastating consequences for others. To address this burden, governments must develop and implement evidence-based and ethically sound strategies and interventions. The World Health Organization (WHO) is committed to supporting countries in this endeavor. In 2010, the World Health Assembly endorsed WHO’s “Global Strategy to Reduce the Harmful Use of Alcohol,” urging countries to strengthen their national responses to public health problems caused by alcohol misuse. Furthermore, WHO’s “Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of NCDs 2013–2020” identifies harmful alcohol use as one of the four key risk factors for NCDs and calls for at least a 10% relative reduction in harmful alcohol use. The inclusion of a target to strengthen the prevention and treatment of substance abuse, including alcohol misuse, in the United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development underscores the importance of reducing alcohol-related harm for societal development. Pricing policies are a key component of the global strategy to reduce harmful alcohol use. WHO’s NCD action plan provides a menu of policy options and cost-effective interventions to assist Member States in implementing actions for the prevention and control of major NCDs. Among these, increasing excise taxes on alcoholic beverages is recognized as one of the most cost-effective interventions available to governments. This resource tool was developed under a Memorandum of Understanding between Thai Health and WHO as part of a broader effort to create technical tools and resource materials supporting the implementation of the global strategy to reduce harmful alcohol use. It aims to enhance the knowledge and competence of public health professionals and alcohol-control policy advocates regarding taxation and pricing policies. By doing so, it seeks to ensure the inclusion of key public health perspectives in the design and implementation of alcohol taxation and pricing policies. Alcohol taxation and pricing policies offer numerous public health, economic, and social benefits. These include generating tax revenue, reducing alcohol consumption and associated harms (both externalities and internalities) among various groups, including young people and heavy drinkers, and preventing the initiation of drinking. This is particularly important in lowand middle-income countries with a high prevalence of lifetime abstainers. Despite ongoing debates about whether taxation should target social drinking or only harmful alcohol use, there are compelling reasons to support government action to apply taxation to general alcoholic beverages to address the problems arising from harmful alcohol use. This resource tool explains several fundamental economic concepts, such as demand-supply equilibrium, price mechanisms of taxation and minimum pricing, price and tax elasticity, and market responses to changes in taxation and pricing policies. It also covers topics such as alcohol excise tax, customs tax, general tax structures, and the limitations of economic models. Alcohol consumption and control through taxation and pricing policies operate via a demand-supply equilibrium mechanism, with elements related to price increases leading to consumption decreases, and vice versa. However, the effects of taxation and pricing policies vary depending on market structures and other contextual factors.
